us17_schools.topic: K-12 schooling: Israel's school streams and funding, US school finance, and outcomes over time (PISA, NAEP, matriculation)

claims.text: OECD PISA 2018 Israel note: Israel first participated in 2002; reading improved since 2001 and mathematics since 2006, most of the gain before 2012; since 2012 no significant change in mathematics and a slight decline in reading; science stable 2006–18; advantaged students outscored disadvantaged by 121 points in reading in 2018 (OECD 89), up from 103 in 2009; about 31% low performers in reading

PISA 2025 (tested March–April 2025, released 8 Sept 2026): Israel reading 474→436, science 465→442, mathematics 458→433; reading the lowest Israel has recorded, below the 2006 low of 439; OECD averages 461 reading, 463 mathematics, 482 science; Israel 31st–33rd of 38 OECD countries; new computational problem-solving domain 444 vs 500
PISA 2025: US reading 490 (down 14 points from 2022, the same fall as the OECD average), mathematics 463; OECD averages 461 reading, 463 mathematics, 482 science

PISA 2025: US science and mathematics not significantly changed from 2022 (or 2015); science above OECD average; US ranked 27th in mathematics, 13th in reading and science; the US had the largest gap between highest and lowest achievers in reading of any participant, and a science gap of nearly 300 points; acting NCES commissioner Matthew Soldner: struggling students 'are not getting the full benefit of what we know how to do'

NAEP 2024 12th grade: average mathematics score lowest since 2005, 45% below Basic, 33% judged ready for college-level maths (37% in 2019); reading lower than on any previous assessment, about 32% below Basic, 12 points higher than in 1992; gap between high and low performers in maths the widest on record

Census FY2024: public school current spending per pupil $17,619, up 6.6% from $16,526 in FY2023 (not inflation adjusted); revenue $994.9bn: state 45.2%, local 43.2%, federal 11.6%; property taxes 63.3% of local revenue; highest New York $31,918, lowest Idaho $11,060

Taub (Blass and Bleikh, 2025), official primary education 2014–2023: the per-student gap between Hebrew state-religious and Arab state education narrowed from about 15% to about 12%; 'Arab State education continues to receive less funding than does Hebrew education'

Education Ministry data analysed by Eli Morgenstern (Ynet, 10 Oct 2026): secular Hebrew state first-grade enrolment fell about 12% 2023–2026 while Haredi first-grade enrolment rose about 11%; in 2025 Arab schools had about 23% of first graders and state-religious about 16%; Haredi schools projected to be the largest stream for first graders by 2030; Haredi and Arab share of preschool children 43.8% (2019) to 48.9% (2026)

IDI 2022: about 373,000 pupils in Haredi education in 2021–22, 25.5% of Hebrew education and 19.5% of all pupils; 14% of Haredi pupils earned a matriculation certificate in 2018–19 vs 83% in the state and state-religious streams; Haredi boys sitting at least one matriculation exam 16% (2008–09) and 15% (2019–20), girls 31% to 59%

IDI study (Finkelstein, July 2025): exempt Haredi schools get about 55% of state-school funding for teaching 55% of the core curriculum; recognised-unofficial schools 75% for 75%; network schools (Shas, UTJ) fully funded and expected to teach all of it; ministry does not enforce the curriculum in exempt or unrecognised schools; 6% of network schools had budget cuts (avg NIS 225,000 in 2023–24); no school closed; at least half do not comply; about 7% of Haredi pupils in state Haredi schools in 2024–25; 76% of Haredi parents of boys said sons learned no English (2022)

Times of Israel, 24 July 2016: ministers voted to repeal clause 10a of the Compulsory Education Law (Yesh Atid's 2013 core-curriculum condition, due 2018) under the 2015 UTJ coalition deal, giving the education minister discretion to fund schools that do not teach core subjects
Times of Israel 2012: in 2011, 48.1% of students completed matriculation; Haredi 8.1%; other Jews 65%; non-Jews 38.2%

EAG 2023: per FTE student, all levels, Israel USD 10,279 (PPP) vs US USD 19,973 vs OECD 12,647; spending primary to tertiary Israel 6.4% of GDP, US 6%, OECD about 5%; upper-secondary teacher statutory salary at 15 years Israel USD 39,321, US 69,641, OECD 53,456; tertiary attainment 25–34: men Israel 36%, US 46%, OECD 41%; women Israel 57%, US 56%, OECD 54%; US K-12 spending ranges from Idaho to DC

EAG 2026 (Ynet): Israel primary class size 27 (OECD 21), public primary 28, lower secondary 30 (OECD 23); NEET 18–24 rose 17%→20% 2015–2025 while OECD fell 16%→13%; teacher pay relative to tertiary-educated workers fell from 86% to 73%
EAG 2024 (ToI): Israel spent 6.1% of GDP on education in 2021 vs OECD 4.9%; 43.1% of Israel's 2022 population aged 0–24 vs OECD 29.7%; 179 school days in grades 1–6

The 74 (15 July 2025): Education Department had just over 4,100 employees in January 2025; the Supreme Court let mass layoffs proceed, effectively halving it; career-technical and adult education moved to Labor; student aid to Treasury and special education to HHS proposed; abolition needs Congress

Times of Israel 2016: about 40,000–50,000 of Israel's 440,000 Haredi pupils attended schools teaching only the ministry minimum of maths and English, receiving 55% of full funding; girls' schools teach maths and English through high school, while many boys' schools stop at sixth grade or below

us17_higher.topic: Higher education: Israel's public universities and uniform tuition vs US college pricing, student debt and the 2025 loan changes

claims.text: CHE: 337,230 students in Israeli higher education in 2021/22 (256,170 bachelor's), about 342,000 expected in 2022/23; women 60%; Arab students over 60,000, 18% of students vs 21% of population; Haredi students 5,500 (2010/11) to 16,575 (2021/22), 4.9% of students vs 13% of population; about a third of bachelor's students from socio-economic clusters 1–4
CHE: Arab share of bachelor's students rose from 10% (2009–10) to 18% (2020–21); master's 6.5% (2011–12) to 16%; PhD 8% (961 students) in 2020–21; Arab students 25,951 (2009–10) to 57,552 (2020–21)

EAG 2026 (Ynet): spending per university student in Israel USD 7,885 (2023, PPP) vs OECD 16,405, fifth from bottom of 33; government share of higher-education spending 38% vs 68%; tertiary attainment 25–34 men 36% (unchanged since 2015, OECD 34%→43%), women 57%

FSA portfolio to 30 June 2026: 42.3m recipients and more than $1.7tn; 9.3m borrowers in default owing $234bn, about 14% of the $1.64tn directly managed portfolio; defaults up about 400,000 in the quarter; Treasury offset and wage garnishment up to 15% of disposable pay; RAP launched July 2026

NY Fed (2013): student loan balances almost tripled 2004–2012 and reached about $994bn in 2013 Q2; borrowers up about 70% 2004–2012; the only household debt that kept rising through the Great Recession, second largest after mortgages

OBBBA loan changes from 1 July 2026: Grad PLUS ends for new borrowers (legacy to 30 June 2029); graduate unsubsidised cap $20,500 a year and $100,000 aggregate; professional $50,000 a year and $200,000; lifetime $257,500; Parent PLUS $20,000 a year and $65,000 per student; new Repayment Assistance Plan and fixed 10–25-year standard plans for new loans; Pell ineligible if SAI exceeds twice the maximum Pell
